name: Adversarial Machine Learning
description: Adversarial examples, poisoning, backdoors, evasion, and robustness of ML models.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from USENIX Security 2018, show a field still mapping out the basic shape of the threat. Several works asked how machine learning could be attacked or formally trusted: "When Does Machine Learning FAIL? Generalized Transferability for Evasion and Poisoning Attacks" (USENIX 2018) unified evasion and poisoning under a single transferability framework, while "Formal Security Analysis of Neural Networks using Symbolic Intervals" (USENIX 2018) pushed in the opposite direction, trying to prove robustness guarantees rather than just demonstrate breakage. At the same time, attacks were already leaving the image domain and hitting real systems, from speech ("CommanderSong: A Systematic Approach for Practical Adversarial Voice Recognition", USENIX 2018) to transfer-learning pipelines ("With Great Training Comes Great Vulnerability: Practical Attacks against Transfer Learning", USENIX 2018). A notable inversion of the threat model also appeared early: "Turning Your Weakness Into a Strength: Watermarking Deep Neural Networks by Backdooring" (USENIX 2018) repurposed backdoors as a defensive ownership tool.

The 2019-2020 period marks a shift from digital perturbations to the physical and hardware substrate of ML systems. "Terminal Brain Damage" (USENIX 2019) and "DeepHammer" (USENIX 2020) showed that flipping a handful of bits in memory via Rowhammer could destroy a network's accuracy, attacking the model where it actually runs rather than at its input. In parallel, attacks moved into the physical sensing pipeline: "Seeing is Not Believing: Camouflage Attacks on Image Scaling Algorithms" (USENIX 2019) exploited preprocessing, and "Towards Robust LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving" (USENIX 2020) demonstrated black-box sensor spoofing against self-driving perception. This era also reframed adversarial techniques as protective tools for ordinary users, most prominently "Fawkes: Protecting Privacy against Unauthorized Deep Learning Models" (USENIX 2020), which cloaked photos to defeat facial recognition scrapers.

By 2021-2022 the community converged on backdoor and poisoning attacks as a central, deployment-relevant concern, especially in pipelines that ingest untrusted data. "Explanation-Guided Backdoor Poisoning Attacks Against Malware Classifiers" (USENIX 2021) used model explanations to craft stealthy poison in crowdsourced threat feeds, and the threat broadened beyond images into text ("T-Miner", USENIX 2021; "Hidden Trigger Backdoor Attack on NLP Models via Linguistic Style Manipulation", USENIX 2022) and into distributed training ("FLAME: Taming Backdoors in Federated Learning", USENIX 2022). Defenses matured alongside, with work like "CADE: Detecting and Explaining Concept Drift Samples for Security Applications" (USENIX 2021) tackling the drift that makes security classifiers brittle over time.

Most recently, attention has tracked the rise of generative models and large language models. "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023) showed that image generators memorize and leak their training data, while "Glaze: Protecting Artists from Style Mimicry by Text-to-Image Models" (USENIX 2023) again turned adversarial perturbations into a protective shield, this time for artists rather than faces, echoing Fawkes years earlier. The frontier has now reached LLM safety directly, with "Making Them Ask and Answer: Jailbreaking Large Language Models in Few Queries via Disguise and Reconstruction" (USENIX 2024) demonstrating efficient query-based jailbreaks. Across six years the area has moved from proving and breaking image classifiers toward securing the full lifecycle of generative and foundation models.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this thread at NDSS treated the neural network itself as the attack surface. Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks (NDSS 2018) set the tone: as people began downloading and reusing public models, an attacker could implant a hidden trigger that stays dormant on normal inputs but hijacks the model on command, all without access to the original training data. The immediate response was defensive. NIC: Detecting Adversarial Samples with Neural Network Invariant Checking (NDSS 2019) treated malicious inputs as anomalies, flagging adversarial examples when they violated invariants the network normally obeys inside its layers.

By 2020 the community saw that adversarial perturbations were not just an evasion trick but a lever for other goals. CloudLeak: Large-Scale Deep Learning Models Stealing Through Adversarial Examples (NDSS 2020) used carefully crafted queries to reverse-engineer commercial cloud models, tying adversarial examples to intellectual-property theft. The real center of gravity then shifted to distributed training. Manipulating the Byzantine (NDSS 2021) showed that optimized model-poisoning attacks could slip past supposedly robust aggregation rules in federated learning, and a parallel line, Data Poisoning Attacks to Deep Learning Based Recommender Systems (NDSS 2021), demonstrated the same corruption of training data in a commercial setting. Defenses answered directly: DeepSight (NDSS 2022) mitigated backdoors in federated learning by inspecting client model updates.

Around the same time the threat left the screen and entered the physical world. Fooling the Eyes of Autonomous Vehicles (NDSS 2022) built robust physical adversarial patches against traffic-sign recognition, and Invisible Reflections (NDSS 2024) later used infrared laser reflections to spoof sign perception invisibly. Backdoors, meanwhile, kept finding new footholds: Backdoor Attacks Against Dataset Distillation (NDSS 2023) proved the trigger survives even compressed, distilled training sets, while Automatic Adversarial Adaption for Stealthy Poisoning Attacks in Federated Learning (NDSS 2024) automated attacks that reshape themselves to dodge whatever defense is deployed, capturing the arms-race character the field had taken on.

The most recent NDSS 2026 papers show the frontier moving to modern model formats and deployment settings. Causal-Guided Detoxify Backdoor Attack of Open-Weight LoRA Models and Rounding-Guided Backdoor Injection in Deep Learning Model Quantization both plant backdoors in the artifacts people actually ship today: shared LoRA adapters for large language models and quantized on-device models. QNBAD (NDSS 2026) even carries backdoor ideas into quantum error-mitigation, while on the defense side PANDORA: Lightweight Adversarial Defense for Edge IoT (NDSS 2026) pushes robustness down to resource-constrained devices. Taken together, the area has grown from a single question about tampered shared models into a broad, adversarial ecosystem spanning federated learning, physical sensing, and the open-weight LLM supply chain.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this list treats adversarial ML as a problem of guarantees and basic attack surfaces. AI2: Safety and Robustness Certification of Neural Networks with Abstract Interpretation (S&P 2018) brought formal verification to neural nets, trying to prove that no small perturbation could flip a classifier's output, while Manipulating Machine Learning: Poisoning Attacks and Countermeasures for Regression Learning (S&P 2018) showed the flip side — attackers corrupting training data to skew a model — and Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning (S&P 2018) established that even a model's training recipe could be extracted. Together these framed the three threats — evasion, poisoning, and model theft — that the field would spend the next decade chasing.

Attention then shifted sharply toward backdoors and toward attacks that work under realistic constraints. Neural Cleanse: Identifying and Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Neural Networks (S&P 2019) became a defining paper on detecting hidden trojan triggers, and Certified Robustness to Adversarial Examples with Differential Privacy (S&P 2019) pushed provable defenses toward scalability. On the attack side, HopSkipJumpAttack: A Query-Efficient Decision-Based Attack (S&P 2020) showed adversaries need only a model's final decisions, and Intriguing Properties of Adversarial ML Attacks in the Problem Space (S&P 2020) confronted the gap between clean math-space perturbations and real, physically realizable inputs. By 2021 this moved fully into the physical and audio world — Invisible for both Camera and LiDAR (S&P 2021) attacked autonomous-driving sensor fusion, and Who is Real Bob? Adversarial Attacks on Speaker Recognition Systems (S&P 2021) targeted voice biometrics, while Detecting AI Trojans Using Meta Neural Analysis (S&P 2021) advanced backdoor detection.

The 2022–2023 window broadened the targets and hardened the defenses. Backdoors reached self-supervised pipelines in BadEncoder: Backdoor Attacks to Pre-trained Encoders (S&P 2022), NLP became a battlefield in Bad Characters: Imperceptible NLP Attacks (S&P 2022), and the federated setting drew both attacks and rebuttals — Back to the Drawing Board (S&P 2022) questioned whether poisoning production federated learning was even practical, answered by a wave of defenses in ELSA, FedRecover, and RoFL (all S&P 2023). Provable and consolidated robustness matured too, with RAB: Provable Robustness Against Backdoor Attacks and the field-surveying SoK: Certified Robustness for Deep Neural Networks (both S&P 2023).

Most recently the center of gravity has moved to generative and foundation models. Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical (S&P 2024) showed that the massive scraped corpora behind modern models are genuinely tamperable, while SneakyPrompt: Jailbreaking Text-to-image Generative Models and Nightshade: Prompt-Specific Poisoning Attacks (both S&P 2024) turned the lens on diffusion models. DataSentinel: A Game-Theoretic Detection of Prompt Injection Attacks (S&P 2025) marks the pivot to LLM-integrated apps and agents. The 2026 slate makes that turn decisive: prompt injection now spans modalities in Hijacking Large Audio-Language Models (S&P 2026), watermarking is attacked from within by WRATH (S&P 2026), retrieval and graph-augmented LLMs are probed in GraphRAG Under Fire and Are LLM-Enhanced Graph Neural Networks Robust Against Poisoning Attacks? (S&P 2026), and the threat surface even reaches the toolchain in Your Compiler is Backdooring Your Model (S&P 2026) — signaling that adversarial ML today is as much about generative systems, agents, and their surrounding infrastructure as about the classic image classifier.

ccs.narrative:
Adversarial machine learning grew from a niche CCS topic in 2018 into one of the conference's dominant threads. The opening papers established both attack primitives and measurement frameworks: Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning (CCS 2018) used CNNs to break Tor defenses, while Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations (CCS 2018) showed that models leak global dataset properties. LEMNA: Explaining Deep Learning based Security Applications (CCS 2018) simultaneously raised the question of whether these complex models could be trusted at all.

In 2019, the battlefield expanded to physical systems and backdoors. Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving (CCS 2019) spoofed LIDAR to inject phantom obstacles into self-driving pipelines, a landmark that made physical adversarial attacks a first-class concern. ABS: Scanning Neural Networks for Back-doors by Artificial Brain Stimulation (CCS 2019) and Latent Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks (CCS 2019) framed the backdoor arms race that would define 2020-2023.

By 2023-2024, generative AI became the new terrain. Narcissus: A Practical Clean-Label Backdoor Attack with Limited Information (CCS 2023) showed backdoors survive even clean-label constraints, DE-FAKE: Detection and Attribution of Fake Images Generated by Text-to-Image Generation Models (CCS 2023) turned attribution into a forensics problem, and Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (CCS 2023) quantified the real-world security cost of AI code generation.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection, clustered in 2018, staked out the two halves of adversarial machine learning that still organize the field: attacks that corrupt a model during training, and attacks that fool it at inference. On the training side, Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks (NDSS 2018) showed that a shared public model could carry a hidden trigger, while Manipulating Machine Learning (S&P 2018) formalized data poisoning against regression learners. Alongside these, a robustness-and-certification thread argued for provable guarantees rather than empirical patches, with AI2 (S&P 2018) using abstract interpretation and Formal Security Analysis of Neural Networks using Symbolic Intervals (USENIX 2018) using interval analysis to bound network behavior. The same year also revealed how tightly adversarial ML is bound to privacy: Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning (S&P 2018) and the property- and membership-inference papers at CCS 2018 showed that models leak their own secrets, and that adversarial-example machinery could be turned into a defense.

The 2019-2020 period turned scattered attacks into named, reproducible problems. Neural Cleanse (S&P 2019) gave defenders a concrete way to detect and reverse-engineer backdoor triggers, and ABS (CCS 2019) and Latent Backdoor Attacks (CCS 2019) pushed the backdoor cat-and-mouse forward. A striking cross-venue development was the move off the screen and into the physical world: Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception (CCS 2019), its black-box follow-up Towards Robust LiDAR-based Perception (USENIX 2020), and Invisible for both Camera and LiDAR (S&P 2021) systematically dismantled autonomous-driving perception, while Intriguing Properties of Adversarial ML Attacks in the Problem Space (S&P 2020) explained why real-world objects are harder to attack than abstract feature vectors. Query-efficient methods like HopSkipJumpAttack (S&P 2020) sharpened the black-box evasion toolkit, and Fawkes (USENIX 2020) flipped adversarial perturbations into a privacy shield against facial recognition.

As training moved to many hands, the attack surface followed. Manipulating the Byzantine (NDSS 2021) optimized model-poisoning attacks against federated learning, and the community answered with defenses such as FLAME (USENIX 2022) and a sober reassessment in Back to the Drawing Board (S&P 2022), which questioned how practical those poisoning attacks really are on production systems. In parallel, meta-level defenses like Detecting AI Trojans Using Meta Neural Analysis (S&P 2021) tried to generalize backdoor detection across unknown triggers.

The most recent work reflects the field's pivot to large generative and foundation models, and its spread into many application niches. Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models (USENIX 2023) showed that generative models memorize and regurgitate their training images, and Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical (S&P 2024) demonstrated that the internet-scale corpora behind modern models can be cheaply corrupted for real. The 2026 NDSS cohort shows both consolidation and fragmentation: backdoors now target the open-weight and quantized model supply chain in Causal-Guided Detoxify Backdoor Attack of Open-Weight LoRA Models and Rounding-Guided Backdoor Injection in Deep Learning Model Quantization, even reaching exotic settings like QNBAD's quantum-noise-induced backdoors, while defenses like PANDORA push adversarial robustness onto resource-constrained edge IoT and ViGText applies vision-language models to deepfake detection. Taken together, the arc runs from fooling a single classifier's pixels to securing an entire distributed, generative, and increasingly LLM-driven machine-learning pipeline.
